tldr: We propose a "co-design framework" that designs a handheld data capture device and a robotic hand together from the ground up, developing the 3-DoF "Koala Gripper" that combines dexterity beyond parallel-jaw grippers with human ease of use.
hero_caption: Appearance of the co-designed handheld data capture device (top: a) and robot-mounted hand (bottom: b). It accomplishes contact-rich tasks like holding an off-the-shelf power drill firmly while pulling the trigger just like a human to fasten a bolt.
overview:
To train robots for dexterous manipulation, large and high-quality demonstration datasets are indispensable. Handheld data collection devices are lightweight and intuitive. However, existing designs often mimic simple 2-finger (parallel-jaw) grippers or unnaturally teleoperate humanoid hands, creating major challenges in manipulation performance and human operator fatigue.

To solve this, the authors introduce a "co-design framework" that considers human physical constraints, ergonomics, and robot actuation/mechanism constraints simultaneously from the start. This methodology gave birth to the "Koala Gripper."

The Koala Gripper has a 3-DoF configuration with two underactuated fingers opposing a single shared thumb. It smoothly transitions between power grasps for securely holding tools and pinch grasps for pinching small parts. In addition, it employs a trigger linkage matching the natural trajectory of human fingers and low-inertia actuators with high backdrivability, minimizing the dynamics gap between data collection and robot execution.

Validation experiments proved an exact match in grasp forces between the handheld device and the robotic hand, along with successful execution of a wide variety of tasks ranging from picking up thin cards to grasping heavy objects and tools. Furthermore, by training a Diffusion Policy on the collected data, the authors demonstrated that the robot can autonomously perform tasks that were challenging for parallel-jaw grippers.
contributions: Systematized a "co-design framework" that simultaneously satisfies the constraints of both the data collection device and the robotic hand from the very beginning.
Developed a novel mechanism combining two underactuated fingers and one mode-switching dual-thumb, achieving diverse grasps (from precision pinching to power grasps of large tools) with only 3 DoFs.

Combined an ergonomic trigger linkage mimicking human finger paths with a highly backdrivable ball screw drive, achieving reduced operator fatigue alongside a low effective mass at the robotic fingertips on the order of tens of grams.
Trained a Diffusion Policy from collected demonstration data, demonstrating autonomous execution of dexterous manipulation skills on a real robot arm.

sections.heading: The Robot Data Dilemma: How Do We Break Beyond Parallel-Jaw Grippers?
sections.summary: Handheld devices are attracting attention for collecting contact-rich manipulation data, but existing solutions suffer from reliance on parallel-jaw grippers and operator fatigue. This work overcomes this barrier by introducing "Koala Gripper," co-designing the handheld collector and the robotic hand together.
sections.details:
To operate robots in unstructured environments such as homes and offices, learning-based control policies like imitation learning are in the spotlight. However, unlike language models or vision models, real-world robotic manipulation data involving physical contact is extremely scarce worldwide.

There are three primary ways to collect data: simulation, teleoperation, and handheld capture devices. Simulation is safe and enables massive generation, but suffers from a severe Sim-to-Real gap in contact-rich tasks. Teleoperation via robots narrows this gap, but the equipment is expensive, lacks haptic feedback, and demands high operator expertise. In contrast, handheld capture devices are inexpensive, portable, and naturally leverage human intuition.

Yet existing handheld devices come with deep compromises. Many are built to match simple parallel-jaw grippers, preventing complex tool use or secure enveloping grasps. Meanwhile, designs that place the human hand directly inside the gripper workspace or rely on exoskeleton gloves quickly exhaust operators and fail to accommodate variations in hand sizes.

To address this, this work introduces a "co-design framework" that simultaneously develops the handheld Capture Device (CD) and the Robotic Device (RD) as a unified pair from the start. This approach shapes the "Koala Gripper" system, balancing human usability with robotic mechanical performance.

sections.heading: A Co-Design Framework for Zero Compromises
sections.summary: Handheld capture devices and robotic hands face completely different constraints: human fatigue/operability versus motor layout/inertia. The authors established a design methodology that solves both simultaneously through an iterative feedback loop centered on common elements.
sections.details:
Co-design begins by defining the target "task requirements." Specifically, it clearly specifies maximum grasp dimensions of target objects, grasp patterns (grasp taxonomies) to execute, multi-modal sensor specifications to measure gripper state, and active workspaces that avoid interference with the environment and the user.

Next, the unique constraints of both the CD (handheld capture device) and RD (robotic execution device) are identified.
- CD constraints: The primary challenge is human ergonomics. The device must minimize fatigue during long collection sessions, support heavy objects, and avoid excessive DoFs that overload the operator's cognitive capacity. It must also provide mechanical advantage over a large finger stroke so human grip strength can generate sufficient grasping force.
- RD constraints: Actuator placement, weight, and inertia of motors and speed reducers. In particular, to safely contact the environment and faithfully replicate motions gathered by the CD, finger inertia must be minimized (yielding low reflected mass and high backdrivability).

By balancing these conflicting constraints, the team runs an iterative feedback loop that continuously refines "Common Elements" such as finger linkage geometries, camera placements, and enclosures. In CAD, both devices reference a single master model, ensuring design changes in one immediately propagate to maintain consistency with the other.

captions.F2: Workflow of the co-design framework. Common Elements are derived from task requirements, and the designs of both the CD and RD are iteratively refined while balancing CD ergonomic constraints against RD actuator constraints.

sections.heading: 3 DoFs Inspired by Koala Paws: Dual-Thumb and Biomimetic Linkage Implementation
sections.summary: To reproduce human hand dexterity with just 3 DoFs, the design adopts two underactuated fingers and one reconfigurable "dual-thumb." It is further engineered with a trigger mechanism tailored to human finger flexion, low-inertia actuators, and specialized fingertip pads.
sections.details:
III-A Gripper Workspace
First, the spatial clearance around the gripper was defined. The bottom side is cleared to pick up objects from tables, the top and back clearances prevent interference with hand tools, and the fingertips extend outward for button pressing and probing. A strict keep-out zone was established to prevent operator hands from colliding with the environment.

III-B Morphology and Grasping Taxonomies
Directly replicating the full DoFs of a human hand makes CD operation overly complex. Thus, a 3-DoF morphology was selected: two independent 1-DoF underactuated fingers opposing a 1-DoF pivoting dual-thumb. Opposing the thumb against two fingers allows stable balancing of rotational moments, which is impossible with parallel-jaw grippers. The thumb linkage toggles between a pinch grasp position (utilizing a kinematic singularity) and a power grasp position (resting against a hard stop), minimizing cognitive load on the operator.

III-C Finger Linkage Mechanism
The fingers use a 9-bar linkage. When the proximal link contacts an object, an underactuated mechanism using an internal spring engages, causing the distal link to automatically curl and wrap around. It eliminates the complex assembly and tension tuning of cable-driven hands, offering superior manufacturability and maintainability.

III-D Finger Actuation (CD and RD)
For the CD, a novel trigger mechanism combines a 4-bar linkage with a linear slider, matching the natural curling trajectory of human fingers. This setup compensates for the dropping mechanical advantage near the finger linkage singularity with a rising trigger mechanical advantage, delivering a flat, low-effort pulling force that yields strong grasping force across the entire stroke. For the RD, TQ frameless motors are paired with a 4 mm lead, highly backdrivable ball screw, matching the human maximum trigger input of 100 N.

III-E Contact Surfaces and Fingernails
The fingertip pads are cast from Shore 30A polyurethane featuring an angled, cantilevered compliance structure. By deforming 2 to 3 mm, they conform to objects with high friction, from slender 7 mm pens to wide 100 mm bottles. Furthermore, rigid metal "fingernails" are embedded at the tips, enabling singulation of thin cards flat on a table and pinching of tiny screws.

III-F Ergonomics and III-G/H System Configuration
Based on hand measurements from 30 individuals, the CD comes in three scaled sizes. Foam pads support the dorsal and palmar surfaces of the hand, freeing the pinky and ring fingers from having to support the weight. The CD also integrates magnetic encoders for finger tracking, a 6-DoF tracking camera (DS80), and three hand-eye cameras, ensuring complete compatibility with RD control signals.

sections.heading: Feather-Light Inertia and 100 N Force: From Force Matching to Autonomous Imitation Learning
sections.summary: Physics simulations confirmed that the RD fingertip effective mass is remarkably light—on the order of tens of grams—and highly backdrivable. The authors also proved an exact grasp force match between CD and RD, demonstrated diverse object grasps, and achieved autonomous task execution using Diffusion Policy.
sections.details:
IV-A System Characterization (Forces and Dynamics)
To ensure the robot side (RD) replicates the compliant contact feel of a human hand (CD), the fingertip reflected mass ($m_{eff}$) was analyzed via finite differences in MuJoCo simulations. Computing the fingertip inertia ellipsoid from the reduced Jacobian $J_{red}$ and reduced mass matrix $M_{red}$ (accounting for actuators and internal springs) revealed that the effective mass in the closing direction is on the order of "tens of grams." It provides outstanding backdrivability, smoothly yielding to external forces.
Furthermore, measuring pinch grasp forces on objects from 10 mm to 40 mm thick showed an exact match between the grasping force produced by a human at maximum input (100 N) on the CD and the grasp force exerted by the RD, proving no force gap exists between data capture and execution.

IV-B Diverse Object Grasping Validation
The Koala Gripper was evaluated across a diverse set of items. It reliably handled diverse daily objects and tools, including using fingernails to lift thin credit cards resting flat on a desk, pinching thin nails, lifting a 25-lb (~11.3 kg) sandbag, grasping a 115 mm diameter 2-liter bottle, and pulling triggers on hammers and spray bottles.

IV-C Imitation Learning Policy Execution
Finally, the authors verified whether imitation learning policies trained on the collected data function properly. A Diffusion Policy was trained taking inputs from three onboard cameras and the 3-DoF gripper state.
- Pasta straining task: 250 episodes collected using the handheld CD.
- Cup destacking task: 100 episodes collected via teleoperation with the RD.
Deploying these policies on a Franka Emika FR3 arm with impedance control demonstrated autonomous, high-precision execution of complex tool and container handling that was previously difficult with parallel-jaw grippers.

sections.heading: Conclusions and Next Steps: Toward Force Feedback and Higher Dexterity
sections.summary: This study established a new paradigm of co-designing handheld data collectors with robotic hands, paving the way for scaling dexterous manipulation learning. Future work includes adding an adduction DoF to the thumb and integrating force/torque sensors for force-reactive policies.
sections.details:
This paper proposed a "co-design framework" that simultaneously incorporates constraints from both data capture devices (CD) and robotic hands (RD), culminating in the "Koala Gripper." Despite a simple 3-DoF design, its blend of an ergonomic trigger and underactuated mechanisms achieved dexterity and ease of data capture that substantially outperform parallel-jaw grippers.

The authors highlight several directions for future advancement:
- Adding a Thumb Adduction DoF: While the current 3-DoF setup covers most grasps, fine in-hand manipulation—such as reorienting parts inside the grasp—requires lateral thumb movement. Adding this DoF is being explored while balancing cognitive load.
- Integrating Grip Force and Wrench Sensing: Currently, the learned policies do not include force feedback. Embedding force sensors into the CD would unlock the Koala Gripper's high torque capabilities to train "force-reactive policies."
- Further Fatigue Reduction: Human fatigue remains the primary bottleneck for data collection throughput. Future revisions will focus on shifting the center of mass closer to the wrist to reduce strain during extended sessions.

takeaways: Simultaneously co-designing both devices around shared common elements from day one—rather than building a handheld device first and adapting a robot later (or vice versa)—is the fastest path to balancing performance with usability.

Instead of pursuing high-DoF hands, focusing on a 3-DoF setup (two underactuated fingers + a reconfigurable dual-thumb) lowers human cognitive load while unlocking far more dexterity than parallel-jaw grippers.

When training robots on contact-rich manipulation tasks via imitation learning, maximizing actuator backdrivability (low effective mass) to mirror the physical compliance of the data collection device (human hand) is critical.
limitations: Because the thumb lacks adduction/abduction (lateral opening motion), it cannot perform in-hand reorientation tasks that require rotating small parts within the grasp.

Grasp forces and fingertip wrenches (contact forces/torques) are not directly measured during data collection, precluding the training of force-controlled policies that finely modulate contact forces.
Although device ergonomics have been substantially improved, operator wrist and arm fatigue during prolonged data collection sessions remains a limiting factor for data scaling.
